title: Does growing up near a college raise schooling and earnings? A replication of Card's (1995) instrumental-variables return to schooling
question: Does a replication of Card (1995) from his public NLS Young Men extract reproduce the instrumental-variables estimate of the return to a year of schooling, using proximity to a four-year college in 1966 as the instrument for completed education?
brief: Replicate the headline two-stage least squares estimate in David Card, 'Using Geographic Variation in College Proximity to Estimate the Return to Schooling' (NBER Working Paper 4832, 1994; published 1995 in Aspects of Labour Market Behaviour: Essays in Honour of John Vanderkamp, University of Toronto Press, with identical tables), using the public data at https://davidcard.berkeley.edu/data_sets/proximity.zip (nls.dat, 3,613 men; the codebook and an example SAS program are in the zip). Follow the paper's sample rule (men with a valid 1976 wage) and its control set, report OLS next to IV, the first stage and the reduced form, and compare with the published numbers. Then pre-specify and report at least one check on instrument strength or validity from the later literature (for example weak-instrument-robust inference, or sensitivity to the exclusion restriction).

data.license: Distributed publicly by the author for research use; no explicit licence stated

requirements: Experience and the control variables are constructed as in the paper; the instrument is the indicator for growing up near a four-year college (nearc4).

Record the replicated 2SLS return to schooling as a result claim with id `iv-return` and its standard error as `iv-return-se`; the first-stage coefficient on the instrument as `first-stage`; and the OLS return to schooling as `ols-return`.
The paper reports the published and replicated estimates side by side, with any difference explained.
The paper states the identifying assumption and what would violate it, and does not describe the IV estimate as the average return for all men.
